svg.aria-label: Diagram: the same fan-out shape drawn twice, side by side, fifteen years apart. On the left, Netflix in 2011 — one caller fanning out roughly one to six across dozens of backing subsystems, at more than a billion calls a day and over 100,000 dependency requests per second at peak. A round trip inside the datacentre is about half a millisecond and across a continent about 150 milliseconds, and the tail is predictable. One dependency goes slow and exhausts the shared thread pool within seconds, silently blocking the five healthy ones. On the right, an agent chain in 2026 — one agent fanning out across plan, retrieve, two tool calls and verify, where every leg is a model call measured in seconds rather than milliseconds and none of them has a dependable tail, so five availabilities multiply and five tails sum. A badge between the two panels reads: same shape, new constants. Along the bottom, the fix is the same both times — put a bus between them: Microsoft rebuilt AutoGen v0.4 on an asynchronous event-driven actor model that decouples how messages are delivered between agents from how the agents handle them, and Confluent states that in a production-grade multi-agent system agents never call each other directly, because over time the system collapses into a distributed monolith. The closing caption reads: the coupling question didn't age — the callees just got slower.

svg.text: The same fan-out, three orders of magnitude slower
